How GPT-2 turns text into vectors

Before a language model can do anything with a sentence, it has to turn the text into numbers. In GPT-2, released by OpenAI in 2019, that is the job of the first layer: it cuts the text into tokens and looks up a list of numbers for each one. Every large language model since starts the same way. This page takes that first layer apart: where the tokens come from, what the table of numbers holds, and how training fills it in.

Everything on this page is computed live in your browser. GPT-2’s real tokenizer runs here, from its own list of 50,000 merges, and a few things are taken from its real table of numbers. To watch the table being learned, a toy model with GPT-2’s structure, shrunk to 6 numbers per token and one layer, trains on the same 30 sentences as the word2vec page. From section 5 on, a bar at the top shows the prediction you have selected. Every interactive has the same controls: reset, play, step, and skip to end. The keyboard drives the one you used last: → steps, space plays or pauses, shift + → skips to the end, and shift + ← resets.

1The problem

A model handles numbers, not letters. word2vec’s answer was to give every word a list of numbers. But a fixed list of words never covers all text. New words, names, typos, other languages and code keep turning up, and a word that isn’t on the list has no numbers at all. Going down to single letters fixes that, but then a sentence becomes a long string of pieces that each mean almost nothing.

GPT-2 splits the difference. Its text is cut into tokens: common words are a single token, rarer ones are built from a few pieces, and anything at all can fall back to single bytes. Its vocabulary has 50,257 tokens, and each one has a number, its token ID.

Type anything and see GPT-2’s tokens

Click a token to see its ID and bytes. A dot · marks a space.

Notice the spaces. A space belongs to the word after it, so ·coffee (with its space) and “coffee” (at the start of a line) are different tokens, with different IDs. Capitals make different tokens too: ·coffee is one token, ·COFFEE is three. A dot marks the space: on this page a token written ·coffee starts with a space.

The toy model on this page uses GPT-2’s own tokens, only far fewer of them. The settings below compare the two.

LayerNorm none before each sublayer, and once more at the top

2Building the vocabulary

GPT-2’s vocabulary was not written by hand. It was learned from text by byte-pair encoding (BPE), a compression trick from the 1990s. Start with every text written as single bytes. Count every pair of neighbouring pieces, merge the most common pair into a new piece, and repeat. Each merge adds one token to the vocabulary.

Before counting, the text is split into words, numbers and punctuation, with each space kept on the word after it, and pairs are never counted across those pieces. That is why tokens are whole words or parts of words, and why ·the and “the” come out as different tokens.

Build a vocabulary from the corpus, one merge at a time

The corpus, in its current tokens

Most common neighbouring pairs

Merges so far

GPT-2 started from the 256 possible byte values, ran 50,000 merges over its training text, and added one special token, <|endoftext|>, which marks where one document ends and the next begins: 256 + 50,000 + 1 = 50,257.

To tokenize new text, GPT-2 does not count anything. It replays its list of merges: within each word, it repeatedly applies whichever available merge it learned earliest, until none applies. A token’s ID is simply 256 plus the place of its merge in that list, so a low ID means a merge learned early, from a very common pair.

Replay GPT-2’s merges on one word

Type a single word. A leading space is part of the word, as it is in running text.

3The token table

A token ID is just a row number. The first layer of GPT-2 is a table with one row for each of the 50,257 tokens and 768 numbers in each row. For every token in the text, it looks up that token’s row. Nothing is calculated: it is a lookup. The table holds 38.6 million numbers, almost a third of GPT-2 small’s parameters.

Here is the toy corpus, cut into GPT-2’s tokens, and its vocabulary.

Before training, every number in the table is random, drawn from a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 0.02. Training then adjusts the rows, as sections 6 to 8 show. Here is one toy row, at the start, middle and end of training, next to the same token’s real row from GPT-2.

One token’s row

In the toy model: 6 numbers

In GPT-2: 768 numbers

Re-rolling draws new random rows and restarts training for the rest of the page.

word2vec gave every word two vectors, an input vector and an output vector, kept in two tables. GPT-2 has one token table, and uses it twice: at the bottom to look up each token, and at the top to score which token comes next (section 6). Sharing one table this way is called weight tying.

Why can GPT-2 get away with one table, when word2vec needed two?
In word2vec, one table would score a word against its own vector. That score is a squared length, always positive, so every word would be predicted next to itself. In GPT-2 the vector scored at the top is not the row that went in at the bottom: it has passed through 12 layers, which have mixed in the rest of the text. So a token’s row is not automatically its own best match. One table also saves parameters: a second 50,257 × 768 table would add 38.6 million.

4Position

The layers that come next, attention layers, see the text as a set of vectors with nothing to say which came first. “the dog walks” and “walks the dog” would look the same. So GPT-2 has a second table, with one row for each position from 0 to 1,023, and adds the position’s row to the token’s row. The sum is the vector that goes into the first layer.

Add the position

Click a token to see its input vector. The same token at another position gets a different input vector.

These position rows are learned, just like the token rows. Nobody told GPT-2 that position 10 is close to position 11. But after training, the rows of nearby positions are nearly the same, and they drift apart smoothly with distance.

GPT-2’s 1,024 position rows

The rows’ three main directions, by position

5Predicting the next token

GPT-2 learns its tables from one task: predict the next token. Every position in a text is one prediction. The vector at position t can look at the tokens up to t, never ahead, and has to say which token comes next. Each sentence here starts and ends with <|endoftext|>, as documents do in GPT-2’s training text, so a sentence of 7 tokens makes 8 predictions: its first token, from <|endoftext|> alone, each token after that, and the end. All of them are trained at once.

Each position predicts the next token

Pick a sentence, then drag the context along it or click a token. The model may look at the tokens inside the box, never ahead.

Every prediction in this sentence

Click a prediction to select it: sections 6 to 8 work through it.

Compare word2vec’s window from the other page: it made pairs of neighbouring words, in both directions. Here the context is everything that came before, and the order matters.

6Scoring every token

At the top of GPT-2, after the last layer, each position has one vector of 768 numbers. Call it h. To predict the next token, GPT-2 scores h against every row of the token table, the same table as in section 3, with the dot product, as word2vec did. That makes 50,257 scores, one for each token. The softmax turns them into probabilities that add up to 1:

pj = escorej / (escore1 + escore2 + … + escoren)

A higher score means a higher probability, and raising one token’s probability lowers all the others. word2vec turned each score into a probability on its own, with the sigmoid. The softmax makes the tokens compete.

Score every token

Scores and probabilities for all 41 tokens

the token that really comes nextevery other token

Real GPT-2, after the same text

As in word2vec, the error is the right answer minus the guess. Now there is one for every token: the label is 1 for the token that really came next and 0 for every other token, so the error is label − p. At the start of training every probability is about 1/41, the model’s best guess when it knows nothing.

7One update

Now the table learns from the error. Each token gets a scaling factor, its error times the learning rate, exactly as in word2vec:

scaling factor=error×learning rateg = (label − p) × α

Then every row of the table moves by its scaling factor times h:

new row=row+scaling factor×hrow ← row + g · h
  • The row of the token that really came next has a positive scaling factor, so it moves toward h. Next time, h will score it higher.
  • Every other row has a negative scaling factor, so it moves away from h, in proportion to how likely the model thought it was. word2vec drew 5 random words to push away. GPT-2 pushes away all 50,256 wrong tokens, the likely ones hardest.

That is the top end. The rows at the bottom learn too. The prediction’s error also travels back down through the layers, and arrives at the input vector as a direction that would have made the prediction better. The input token’s row and the position’s row both move a small step that way. On this page that direction is computed exactly, by working back through the toy’s one layer.

8Adding up an update

A sentence makes several predictions, and every one of them moves every row of the table a little. The model works out all of these parts first, with the table as it stands, then adds them up and changes each row once. This is one training step.

Add up the parts for one row

Applying the update

How far every row moves in this step

A row gets parts from three roles: as the right answer at some positions, as a wrong answer at all the others, and as an input wherever its token appears in the sentence. One GPT-2 step adds up the parts from 512 × 1,024 = 524,288 predictions.

9Two tokens drawing together

“coffee” and “tea” never appear in the same sentence. But the same tokens come before them, ·hot, ·the and ·my, and the same tokens follow, ·with, ·every and ·is. So the vectors h that should predict them are alike, which pulls both rows the same way at the top, and as inputs both rows should lead to the same predictions. Their rows drift together, through the same kind of shared company word2vec used.

Any two rows lie together in one flat plane, so they can be drawn at their true lengths with the true angle between them. Compare the start, middle and end of training, and try a token that shares no company with ·coffee, such as ·dog.

Compare two tokens’ rows

10Training at scale

Now run the toy over the whole corpus, 120 times, one sentence per step: 3,600 steps. The loss is the error as the model measures it: −log p of the token that really came next, averaged over the sentence’s predictions. It starts at log 41 ≈ 3.7, a uniform guess among 41 tokens.

Train the toy model on the corpus

Loss per token

Learning rate α

The loss cannot fall to zero, because the corpus doesn’t always say what comes next. After ·hot, the corpus has ·coffee twice, ·tea twice, ·drink once and the end of the sentence twice, so the best possible guess there splits its probability.

11Inside GPT-2’s table

The real table, after training on 40 GB of text, holds the same kind of structure at a far larger scale. Here are the nearest neighbours of any word in it, by the angle between rows. The rows themselves come straight from GPT-2’s released weights.

Nearest neighbours in GPT-2’s table

The page looks up the token for the word with a space in front, as it would appear mid-sentence. Neighbour lists are included for 14,940 common word tokens.

Many of the neighbours are the same word in another form: capitalized, plural, or without its space. GPT-2 has to learn for itself that ·coffee and ·Coffee mean the same thing, and puts their rows close together. The rest are related words: for ·coffee, ·espresso, ·caffeine and, as in the toy, ·tea.

The table has other habits. Its rows are not spread evenly in every direction: they all share a large common offset, so two random rows have a cosine similarity of about 0.27 instead of 0. Subtract the average row and that drops to about 0. And some rows barely moved at all. A token’s row only gets the pull toward h when that token comes next, which some tokens almost never did. The tokenizer seems to have been built from different text than the model was trained on, so it has tokens like ·TheNitrome, ·RandomRedditor and ·externalToEVA: strings common in the tokenizer’s text that hardly appear in the model’s. They were found in 2023 as “glitch tokens”, which confuse the model. Their rows got almost no training, and sit close to the average row.

How far each row sits from the average row

12The table is static

A token’s row is the same wherever the token appears. “plot” gets the same numbers in “the garden plot” and in “the secret plot”. Telling the two apart is the job of the 12 layers that follow: each layer mixes information from the other tokens into each vector. At the bottom the two “plot” vectors are identical; layer by layer they move apart.

One word, two meanings, through GPT-2’s layers

So the first layer is a starting point. It gives each token what is true of it everywhere, and the rest of the network builds what it means here.

Footnotes

  1. Radford, Wu, Child, Luan, Amodei and Sutskever, “Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners” (2019). GPT-2: byte-level BPE with merges kept within character categories, a 1,024-token context, batches of 512, WebText.
  2. Sennrich, Haddow and Birch, “Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units”, ACL (2016), brought byte-pair encoding, first a compression method (Gage, 1994), to language modelling.
  3. Press and Wolf, “Using the Output Embedding to Improve Language Models”, EACL (2017), on tying the input and output tables. GPT-2’s released code computes its scores with the token table itself.
  4. Rumbelow and Watkins, “SolidGoldMagikarp (plus, prompt generation)” (2023), on GPT-2 and GPT-3’s “glitch tokens”, such as ·SolidGoldMagikarp (a single token, as section 2 shows), and their rows near the centre of the table.
  5. Ethayarajh, “How Contextual are Contextualized Word Representations?”, EMNLP (2019), on how GPT-2’s vectors share a common direction and grow more context-specific in higher layers. Section 12 subtracts each layer’s average vector, taken over a dozen ordinary sentences, before comparing, so the shared offset doesn’t make every pair look alike. Its layer 12 is the last layer’s output before GPT-2’s final LayerNorm.
  6. The toy model, corpus and seeds are this page’s own. The toy adds up its loss over a sentence’s predictions, where GPT-2 averages over a batch; that only changes the scale of the learning rate. It uses GELU in its MLP, as GPT-2 does, and no LayerNorm. Sections 6 to 8 look at the model just before the selected sentence’s update in the first pass (start), the 60th (middle) and the 108th of 120 (end), where the learning rate has not yet shrunk to almost nothing. Across 100 initialization seeds, ·coffee and ·tea ended up as each other’s nearest neighbours 99 times, and ·dog and ·cat 99 times too.
